Photograph: David Goldman/AP Technology Flock Safety tries to curb police abuse of its surveillance cameras after scandals CEO announces steps after reports that system is used to target immigrants or people seeking out-of-state abortions Johana Bhuiyan Thu 13 Aug 2026 16.20 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 16.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google For nearly a decade, the company Flock Safety has gradually built out a network of cameras across the US that allows law enforcement officials to conduct about 20bn license plate scans every month. In that time, the company had largely left the decision to turn on safety measures up to its customers. Many of those organizations did not turn them on. Now, the company is doing damage control. Garrett Langley, Flock’s CEO, announced on Thursday that the company would begin mandating that law enforcement agencies switch on features that could help audit the way individual officers use its tracking capabilities. It had been reported that more than 50 law enforcement officers were accused of or charged with abusing Flock’s camera system, including to stalk ex-partners. “These changes reflect years of work and deliberation,” Langley wrote in a blogpost announcing the new guardrails. “They are not the end of that work, but simply the continuation of our commitment to both safety and privacy.” Four months ago, the company introduced a voluntary feature called Audit Assistance, which flags “abnormal activity” for administrative review. Langley said on Thursday that about a third of its customers turned it on. Now, the rest of its customers, which include law enforcement agencies, retailers , universities , and homeowner associations , have until the end of the year to activate it. Under the new system, when the system flagged behavior as “abnormal”, the user would be automatically suspended, pending a review. The announcement did not include details about what qualified as “abnormal”. The company will also now allow law enforcement agencies to restrict the information offered to other agencies on specific offenses rather than giving free rein to the agencies that they partner with to access all of their license plate scans. Now, the company wrote, agencies can limit the scans they share with other cities or states to specific types of investigations like stolen vehicle or missing persons cases. The feature in part addresses years of reports that the company’s system had been used to target immigrants or people seeking out-of-state abortions, at times in violation of state or local laws. In addition, Flock will now automatically set its license plate scan retention time to seven days, down from its existing default of 30 days. However, agencies can identify certain scans as part of a longer-term investigation if they want to maintain that data for longer, the company said, and can continue to choose “the retention period that fits its public safety strategy”. These concerns have grown since the US supreme court’s reversal of its Roe v Wade decision guaranteeing the right to abortions. The Guardian found in 2022 that some California police departments were sharing license plate reader data with states where abortion is banned, potentially in violation of California’s own out-of-state data-sharing laws. At the time, a Flock executive said that the company’s mission was to “eliminate crime” and that crime was defined by the state or municipality a camera operates in. Privacy experts question whether these features are enough to protect the more than 6,000 communities where these Flock cameras are situated. “I don’t think there’s such a thing as ‘mass surveillance, but with guardrails’. Ultimately, networked cameras sprinkled across the country are incompatible with a free society,” said Chris Gilliard, author of the forthcoming book Luxury Surveillance . Reports of misuse of Flock’s system as well as concerns over privacy infringement have dogged the company for years but have only recently had a significant impact on it. The company was vaulted into the public’s consciousness after Amazon Ring announced and then cancelled its plan to integrate Flock’s license plate reader technology into its doorbell cameras. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion Since then, there’s been a growing citizen uprising against Flock cameras, prompting Langley to call vigilantes taking down Flock cameras “terrorists” and then apologize. Now, more than 80 cities have dropped or are publicly considering dropping their contracts with Flock. Inside the growing vigilante movement to knock out Flock surveillance cameras Read more But Robert Frommer, a senior attorney at the Institute of Justice, which is representing the plaintiffs in two federal lawsuits against the warrantless use of license plate readers, said Flock’s new features only amount to police departments policing themselves. “This is yet more window dressing,” said Frommer. “Flock suggests that police departments limit their retention periods to seven days, while admitting that decision is still entirely up to the police departments themselves.” 38:58 Inside the vigilante movement destroying Flock cameras – Stateside with Kai and Carter Explore more on these topics Technology Surveillance Road transport news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty Images Movies Eva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies aged 102 Landmark roles were in 50s classics directed by Elia Kazan and Alfred Hitchcock, before going on to play Superman’s adoptive mother in later life Eva Marie Saint – a life in pictures Her best films – ranked Andrew Pulver Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.24 EDT Last modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 17.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Eva Marie Saint, one of the last survivors of Hollywood’s golden age of the 1940s and 50s, has died aged 102. Her screen work spanned six decades: Saint made her screen debut opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront, starred in Alfred Hitchcock’s celebrated thriller North by Northwest, and in one of her last screen appearances played Superman’s adoptive mother Martha Kent in the 2006 superhero film Superman Returns . A family spokesman said on Tuesday that Saint had died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles. Eva Marie Saint – a life in pictures Read more Born in 1924 in New Jersey to a Quaker family, Saint had an early career as a jobbing radio and TV performer that was chronicled in a 1949 feature in Life magazine which started with the prophetic words: “The name of Eva Marie Saint may someday be a household word” – it followed her struggles to gain a foothold in the entertainment industry. By the early 50s she was making some headway, appearing in 1953 in both the original telecast and the premiere Broadway production of the Horton Foote play The Trip to Bountiful. Saint told the Santa Barbara Independent that On the Waterfront director Elia Kazan spotted her in The Trip to Bountiful and invited her to audition by improvising a scene with Marlon Brando. Saint said she found the experience difficult, but was offered the role of Edie Doyle, Brando’s love interest, in the hardhitting drama about mob union activities; she would go on to win the Oscar for best supporting actress in 1955. Eva Marie Saint’s best films – ranked Read more After this meteoric success, Saint quickly began securing a wide variety of leading roles. She starred opposite Bob Hope in That Certain Feeling, played a woman married to a secret drug addict in the Fred Zinnemann-directed issue picture A Hatful of Rain and co-starred with Elizabeth Taylor in the period western Raintree County. Saint then achieved the highly coveted role opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s 1959 spy classic North by Northwest: secret agent Eve Kendall, “a blond who has all the answers”. She said in a TCM interview that she got her career-defining role – partly – by wearing beige and white gloves to a lunch appointment with Hitchcock. Saint kicked off the 1960s by playing American nurse Kitty Fremont in Exodus, the hit adaptation of Leon Uris’s novel about the creation of the state of Israel, but subsequently eased up on her workload to prioritise her young family. In 1962 she appeared opposite Warren Beatty in All Fall Down as a woman infatuated with Beatty’s drifter, starred as Richard Burton’s wife in The Sandpiper in 1965 alongside Elizabeth Taylor and played a journalist who has an affair with Yves Montand’s race driver in Grand Prix in 1966. View image in fullscreen With Cary Grant in North by Northwest. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Alamy Despite critical acclaim for her role in the 1970 infidelity drama Loving alongside George Segal, Saint’s film parts largely dried up in the 70s and 80s, with the actor instead turning to TV movies and guest appearances. Sporadic film appearances ensued after a “comeback” in the 1986 Tom Hanks/Jackie Gleason comedy Nothing in Common; later appearances included as Sam Shepard’s mother in the Wim Wenders-directed western Don’t Come Knocking in 2005, and a year later she was cast in Superman Returns – where she was “reunited” with On the Waterfront star Brando, whose estate gave permission for 1978 footage to be used in the film after his death in 2004. Saint worked more consistently in TV, winning a best supporting actress Emmy award for the 1990 mini-series People Like Us, adapted from Dominick Dunne’s novel. Her final onscreen role was in Winter’s Tale as the sister of the seemingly immortal Colin Farrell. Saint married Jeffrey Hayden in 1951 and had two children; they remained together until his death in 2016. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/11/08/rtl-.text: Három ügyben is nyomoz a rendőrség, amelyek a korábbi Honvédelmi Minisztérium beszerzéseit érintik – közölte az RTL Híradójával az ügyészség. A három, hűtlen kezelés gyanúját felvető ügyről még szeptemberben beszélt Ruszin-Szendi Romulusz miniszter, miután átvilágították az előző vezetés szerződéseit. A honvédelmi miniszter szerint Szalay-Bobrovniczky Kristóf előző honvédelmi miniszter a külföldi magáncélú útjain – például vadászatok során – is igénybe vette a neki járó személyi védelmet, ami 32 millió forintjába került az államnak. Egy másik alkalommal pályáztatás nélkül, 12 milliárd forintért bíztak meg egy angol céget azzal, hogy írjon szabályzatot bizonyos katonai eszközök használatáról, tartson vezetői tréningeket és angol mintára tervezzen egyenruhát. Az egyenruhát végül nem rendszeresítették. Ruszin-Szendi nem a cég által elvégzett tanácsadói munka minőségét kifogásolta, hanem az erre elköltött 12 milliárdot sokallta. A harmadik ügy pedig Szalay-Bobrovniczky magáncélra bérelt szolgálati autójával volt kapcsolatos, ami havi 600-800 ezer forintba kerülhetett. Mindhárom ügyben hűtlen kezelés gyanúja miatt tett feljelentést szeptemberben a minisztérium. Az RTL érdeklődött az ügyészségnél, hogy indult-e valamilyen eljárás a feljelentések nyomán. A hivatal közölte: a Fővárosi Nyomozóügyészség mindhárom ügyben nyomoz, részleteket viszont nem árultak el. A Fidesz az RTL-nek azt mondta a fejleményre, hogy továbbra is fenntartják a korábbi kijelentésüket, miszerint „a bukott vezérkari főnök támadásait” visszautasítják. Az egyenruhákról hozzátették, hogy a kormányváltás miatt nem vezették be, és hogy szerintük Szalay-Bobrovniczky a magáncélú útjain is jogszerűen kapott személyi védelmet.
